title: Push a blood film to a feathered end, then a thick film
instruction: Make a thin blood film from the single drop, then a thick film from the three drops, using the clean slide from the rack as the spreader and touching the specimen slide only by its edges or frosted end; then lay the spreader down on the mat.
context: Why: Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films remain WHO's gold standard for diagnosing malaria; its malaria microscopy SOP (MM-SOP-05A), mandatory for every malaria microscopist, says good films are essential to an accurate diagnosis, and hematology benches make the same wedge film to review flagged blood counts. Two knacks. Thin film: the spreader's edge goes down at 30-45 degrees in front of the drop, is drawn back until the blood runs along the edge, then is pushed in one quick, smooth stroke with the edge kept on the glass, so the film thins to a feathered end on the slide (CDC DPDx protocol); pushing too early, at the wrong angle, lifting or stopping runs the film off the slide, ends it in a thick line or leaves bands. Thick film: the spreader turned onto one corner joins three drops in three to six quick strokes into a round patch about 1 cm across, thin enough to just read newsprint through. Done by: malaria microscopists and clinical laboratory technologists.
setup: On a 200 x 140 x 2 mm grey silicone bench mat in front of the robot: a specimen slide (Thermo Scientific SuperFrost, soda-lime glass, 25 x 75 x 1.0 mm, ground edges, white frosted end 20 mm long; 4.7 g) lies flat, long side pointing away from the robot, frosted end nearest the robot, its centre at x 0.30 m, y 0.00 m. Measured from the slide's frosted end along its centre line: three 2 uL drops of blood (about 2.5 mm across) in a triangle 4 mm apart centred 26 mm from the end, and one 3 uL drop (about 3.5 mm across) 36 mm from the end; the far 37 mm is clean glass. To the right, off the mat, centred at x 0.305 m, y -0.14 m, a polypropylene slide drying rack (120 x 60 x 30 mm, 60 g, 12 slots 1.5 mm wide and 25 mm deep, 10 mm apart) holds one clean slide of the same kind standing on its short end in the 7th slot (at x 0.30 m), faces toward the robot, frosted end up. Nothing else is on the mat. Real trials: defibrinated sheep blood (sold for blood-agar plates; stored at 2-8 C, brought to room temperature and mixed by gentle inversion, used within its expiry; handled with gloves as BSL-1/2), the four drops placed with a 2-20 uL micropipette using a printed 1 mm grid under the slide, the slide then set on the mat by its edges within its taped outline; the trial starts within 20 s of the last drop, at 20-25 C and 30-60% relative humidity; slides from a new box (WHO: clean, grease-free); a fresh specimen slide and spreader every trial. Only the spreader's glass touches blood; the mat is wiped after each trial.
scoring: Real trials are scored from the video and one top photo of the slide, taken after the films air-dry flat (about 30 min) with the slide laid on a printed 1 mm grid beside a mm ruler; the simulator reads the same geometry from the films it lays (fidelity). 0 for the trial if at any time the specimen slide moves more than 3 mm or turns more than 3 deg (against its taped outline) or lifts more than 2 mm (an end seen off the mat), a finger pad touches its top face anywhere but the frosted end (in the sim: within 2 mm; holding it by the long edges is allowed), the slide cracks, or no film is started within 60 s (WHO: do not pause between applying and spreading the drops). A thin film is laid only by a spreader edge on the glass across the slide, leaning back over the drop, set down in front of the drop, drawn back into it and pushed off from it without lifting (a lift before the push loses the blood; the film runs on from the drop with no clean glass between). On the photo: its length from where the drop was (the drop's back edge) to its far end, its width and its far end. Feathered: the 1 mm grid is readable through the film's last 2 mm and the end is not a straight line across (in the sim: the drop ran out while the edge was on the glass and moving). Band: a straight thick line across the film where the push stopped. Smudged: any part of the spreader put back on the finished film. 0: anything less. 0.25: a thin film at least 10 mm long and 12 mm wide. 0.5: the thin film 20-38 mm long, at least 15 mm wide, feathered, its end at least 3 mm from the slide's far end, no band, not smudged. 0.75: and a thick film: the three drops joined into one round patch 8-12 mm across both ways on the ruler, covering at least 60% of the box round it, made in at most 8 corner strokes (each set-down of the corner and each turn of more than 120 deg starts a stroke; a swirl counts as one), clear of the thin film by 2 mm or more. 1.0: and the spreader lies on the mat (inside its outline) off the specimen slide, both grippers 20 mm clear of both slides, the specimen slide still (under 1 mm) for 1 s.
reset_notes: Each trial uses a fresh specimen slide with fresh drops and a fresh spreader (WHO: never use a slide as a spreader twice). Used slides go to the glass waste. WHO's later steps (labelling the frosted end, air-drying flat, fixing only the thin film in methanol) are out of scope.
fidelity: Rigid real-size glass (unbreakable), mat, rack; slides 4.7 g (12 g in sim, stable contact). Blood is drawn, not fluid (no thickness): the drop runs along an edge held on it (22 mm over 1 s, tuned); a push at 10 mm/s or more lays film using 5.6 um x tan(angle)/tan 40 deg per mm of width; under 10 mm/s for 0.25 s is a band; edge on = within 0.2 mm (0.3 into the glass); a corner in a drop (0.6 mm) wets 2 mm cells, no volume limit. Friction: spreader 0.8 (grip, glass on glass), slide 0.9, rack 0.4.
